content: Latin, known as lingua Latīna, is an ancient Indo-European language that was originally spoken in Ancient Rome. It served as the de facto international language of science and scholarship in much of Europe until the 17th century. The language spread widely across the Mediterranean and Europe through Roman conquests. Over time, Latin evolved into the Romance languages, including French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian, which later spread to the Americas and Africa. Latin is traditionally divided into two forms: Classical Latin, used in formal prose and poetry, and Vulgar Latin, which consisted of regional dialects that eventually developed into the Romance languages. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Latin became the official language of the Catholic Church and the lingua franca of educated individuals in Western Europe. By the 16th century, Latin began to decline as a spoken language, though Vulgar Latin persisted in regional dialects, which became the foundation of modern Romance languages. Ecclesiastical Latin remains in use within the Catholic Church, and Latin vocabulary continues to be employed in fields such as science, law, and academia. Classical Latin, the literary form of the language, is still taught in schools, often alongside Greek in the study of Classics, though its prominence has diminished since the early 20th century. The Latin alphabet, with its modern adaptations, is the most widely used writing system globally. The Latin language belongs to the Italic branch of the Indo-European family. Its alphabet was derived from the Old Italic script, which itself originated from the Greek alphabet. Latin was introduced to the Italian peninsula by the Latins, who settled in the region of Latium near the Tiber River in the 9th or 8th century BCE. During its early development, Latin was influenced by the Etruscan language of northern Italy. While surviving Roman literature is primarily written in Classical Latin, the spoken language of the Roman Empire's common people was Vulgar Latin, which differed significantly in grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation. Although Latin was the official language of the Roman Empire, Greek was the preferred language of the educated elite, as much of the literature and philosophy studied by Romans originated from Greek authors. In the Byzantine Empire, which emerged from the eastern half of the Roman Empire, Greek eventually replaced Latin as the official language. The Latin alphabet, used by the Romans, has been adapted for numerous modern languages, including English, Spanish, and French. Ancient Roman writing lacked punctuation, lowercase letters, and interword spacing, though dots were occasionally used to separate words. The Romans also did not use the letters j and u, and they employed apices to indicate long vowels. Roman cursive script has been discovered on wax tablets, such as those found at Vindolanda near Hadrian's Wall in Britain. The expansion of the Roman Empire facilitated the spread of Latin across Europe. Over time, Vulgar Latin began to diverge into distinct regional dialects, which eventually became the Romance languages. By the 9th century, these languages were primarily spoken rather than written, as Latin remained the dominant written language. For example, Latin was the official language of Portugal until 1296, when it was replaced by Portuguese. Among the Romance languages, Italian is the most conservative in terms of vocabulary, while Sardinian is the most conservative in terms of phonology. The Romance languages differ from Latin in several ways, such as the loss of case endings in most words (except for Romanian, which retains some case distinctions) and the development of stress-based pronunciation patterns. English, though a Germanic language in grammar, has a significant portion of its vocabulary derived from Latin, often through French and Anglo-Norman influences. During the medieval period, Latin terms entered English through ecclesiastical usage, and during the Renaissance, many new words were coined from Latin and Greek roots. Latin is a synthetic, fusional language, meaning that grammatical relationships are expressed through affixes attached to word stems. Nouns, adjectives, and pronouns are declined to indicate gender, number, and case, while verbs are conjugated to express person, number, tense, voice, mood, and aspect. Latin nouns have six primary cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, and ablative, each serving specific syntactic functions. A seventh case, the locative, is used for indicating location, though it is less common and primarily applies to place names. Latin verbs are categorized into four main conjugations, based on the ending of their present active infinitive forms. There are six tenses (present, imperfect, future, perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect), four moods (indicative, subjunctive, imperative, and infinitive), two voices (active and passive), and six grammatical persons (first, second, and third, in both singular and plural). Verbs are identified by four principal parts, which provide the necessary forms for conjugation. Latin instruction in modern education focuses primarily on reading and translating texts rather than spoken communication. However, the Living Latin movement advocates for teaching Latin as a spoken and written language, similar to modern languages. This approach aims to enhance understanding of Latin literature and poetry by emphasizing the sounds and rhythms of the language. Living Latin is taught in institutions such as the Vatican and some universities, and organizations like the National Junior Classical League promote Latin studies among students. Latin translations of modern works, such as Harry Potter and Winnie the Pooh, have been created to spark interest in the language. In contemporary times, Latin remains widely used in specialized fields such as medicine, biology, law, and philosophy. It is the preferred language for scientific nomenclature and is used in legal terms and abbreviations. The Catholic Church continues to use Latin in official contexts, and the language is sometimes employed in films and mottos. For example, the United States Marine Corps' motto, Semper fidelis, is Latin for always faithful. Some universities still conduct graduation ceremonies in Latin, preserving its legacy in academic traditions.
